title: Closed Ruy Lopez
subtitle: Morphy Defense — the knight tour that never stops working
summary: The Closed Ruy Lopez is where the family study's opening ideas turn into decades of grandmaster theory: White spends move after move on prophylaxis before ever pushing the center, and the reward is a slow squeeze that has produced more World Championship points than any other single tabiya. Learn the famous knight regrouping that gives the position its shape, and the three named systems Black uses to answer it.

metadata.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Closed Defense

rootAnnotations.title: What this lesson teaches
rootAnnotations.body: The family study, The Ruy Lopez, walks the Closed complex only as far as 9...Na5 10.Bc2 c5 11.d4 — one of several 9th-move systems Black can choose. This lesson picks up at the real branch point, move 9, and follows the modern main line (the Breyer Variation) three knight moves deeper into the maneuvering that makes this the most analyzed structure in chess, while naming the other two major 9th-move systems that share the same first eight moves.

annotations.body: c3 prepares the central break d4 and reserves c2 as a retreat square for this bishop. The family study's own trap reference applies here too: pushing d4 before this preparation is exactly how a player falls into the Noah's Ark Trap — c3 is what makes the eventual break safe.

annotations.title: The move that opens three roads
annotations.body: As in the family study, h3 rules out ...Bg4 before White ever threatens d4. What comes next is Black's choice of system: the position from here has supported three of the most important named variations in opening theory, all sharing this exact tabiya.
The knight retreats to its starting square, seemingly undoing three moves of development. What could possibly be worth that?

annotations.title: The Breyer Variation
annotations.body: Named for Gyula Breyer and mocked for decades before Karpov turned it into a model plan, this is the modern main line. The knight was awkwardly placed on c6, blocking the c-pawn and doing nothing for the center; from b8 it reroutes to d7, where it supports both ...c5 and a future ...Nf8-g6 or ...e5-based regrouping. Time is spent now so the pieces end up on better squares than a direct route ever offered.

annotations.title: The Chigorin Variation
annotations.body: Named for Mikhail Chigorin, this is the classical main system: the knight chases the b3-bishop off its diagonal before Black commits to a central break. The continuation 10.Bc2 c5 11.d4 Qc7 is exactly the line the family study, The Ruy Lopez, follows to its own final position — this catalog entry names the system that study only played through.

annotations.title: The Zaitsev Variation
annotations.body: Kasparov's long-time weapon of choice. The bishop develops to its natural diagonal at once instead of committing the queenside knight first, keeping options open about whether it supports ...c5, a central ...d5 break, or simply sits ready on the long diagonal.
The break everything since move 9 prepared, now landing at full strength.
The point of the Breyer regrouping arrives: the knight heads to d7, a far better post than c6 ever was, freeing the c-pawn to support ...c5 without blocking anything.
The bishop finally develops now that b5 and d5 are both securely defended — completing the same fianchetto the Zaitsev plays immediately, but here after the knight maneuver instead of before it.

annotations.title: Clearing the road for d5
annotations.body: The bishop steps off b3 before Black can gain a tempo against it with ...c4, tucking onto a square where it will support a future d4-d5 advance and keep an eye on the long diagonal toward h7.

annotations.title: The famous knight tour
annotations.body: Nb1-d2-f1-g3 is the single most recognizable maneuver in the Ruy Lopez. The knight had no future on d2 once its central-support job was done, so it heads for g3, where it eyes f5 and h5 and supports a kingside buildup that a knight on the rim could never provide.
The knight completes its tour, eyeing f5 and h5 and supporting a future kingside buildup that a knight on the rim could never provide.

annotations.title: The Breyer tabiya
annotations.body: This exact position — reached by transposition from dozens of move orders — has been played thousands of times at grandmaster level. White's pieces all point at the kingside and center (Ng3 eyes f5, Bc2 eyes h7, Re1 backs up e4); Black answers with the mirror idea, preparing ...Bg7 to cover f5 and h5 before White can use them. For a full game showing this entire strategic complex play out from these first eight moves, see Karpov vs Unzicker.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons to carry out of this study: a knight can improve by retreating, if the square it lands on afterward is genuinely better (Nb8-d7 is not a wasted move, it's a route); prophylactic moves like h3 exist to remove the opponent's options before creating your own threats, not instead of them; and the three named 9th-move systems — Breyer, Chigorin, Zaitsev — are not separate openings so much as three answers to the same question Black must face once h3 has been played.
